implementation_barriers.barrier: Labour organisation and historical constraints require all furnaces to operate during the night for morning tapping
implementation_barriers.evidence_quote:
Currently, for historical reasons and because of labour and
energy costs, the pouring of molten metal is conducted at the
beginning of the ﬁrst shift in the morning, which means that all
furnaces have to operate during the night.

implementation_barriers.barrier: Energy-efficient sequential melting is negated by higher peak-hour electricity cost
implementation_barriers.evidence_quote:
the foundry currently performs sequential melting during the
peak hours, thus the energy saving is cancelled out by the higher
hourly cost.

implementation_barriers.barrier: Poor profitability of the holding-furnace investment because existing furnaces would be left unused
implementation_barriers.evidence_quote:
The lack of
proﬁtability is due to the fact that, in the considered scenario, two
furnaces which are already owned by the foundry are, de facto,
unused.

reviewer_notes: Methodology paper with two illustrative applications: a literature-derived representative container glass furnace (A1) and a grey/spheroidal cast iron foundry (A2). Additional fitted models exist but were not enveloped separately to avoid duplication: the melting-shop regression Ein = 0.6129 m (Eq. 30, system boundary B, p.10) which is analogous to furnace #1 model M2, and a representative overall foundry SEC of 675 kWh/t (p.10). The ~14% energy saving from scheduling/holding-furnace optimisation (Table 4, p.12) is a deterministic scenario comparison and was attached to M3 as the closest overall model. The evidence for two years of monthly data spans the page 6/7 break ('...through the statistical approach, two' | 'years of monthly data...'); the contiguous page-7 portion was quoted, and span_months=24 is marked requires inference.
